query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy (Cantor alloy) exhibits superior ductility because its single-phase FCC structure provides numerous active slip systems that promote dislocation mobility and twinning during deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy in an as-solid-solution, single-phase FCC microstructure.
generation.intervention: Conduct in situ nano-mechanical tensile testing (e.g., TEM-based or synchrotron diffraction during deformation) along with atomistic simulations.
generation.conditions: Ambient temperature and typical mechanical loading (tensile deformation) under standard conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The inherent face‐centered cubic crystal structure providing multiple slip systems and a favorable stacking fault energy.
generation.mechanism: Under load, the FCC structure facilitates dislocation glide and twinning, which absorb deformation energy and delay crack propagation, leading to improved ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy is expected to show significantly higher plastic deformation before failure compared to less ductile materials, as the multiple activation pathways (dislocation motion and twinning) enhance work hardening and stave off fracture.
generation.baseline: Classical FCC metals (e.g., copper or aluminum) that also exhibit ductility, but the complexity and uniformity of the high-entropy system are predicted to further enhance the ductile behavior.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected under ambient and moderate deformation conditions; at extreme temperatures or strain rates, phase stability or other mechanisms (e.g., phase transformation) may alter the ductile response.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative link between FCC structure and ductility is well supported, precise quantitative relationships related to stacking fault energy and detailed dislocation behavior require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ TEM tensile testing on CoCrFeMnNi samples at ambient temperature along with atomistic simulations to correlate observed dislocation dynamics and twinning with stress–strain behavior.
measurements: Stress–strain curves to determine the onset of yielding and ultimate tensile elongation
Real-time TEM imaging of dislocation motion and twin formation
Quantitative evaluation of stacking fault formation during deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CoCrFeMnNi alloy does not exhibit the expected high ductility characterized by significant plastic deformation (via dislocation glide and twinning) relative to known FCC metals, or if the microstructural mechanisms do not align with the predictions, the hypothesis would be falsified.

Nanomaterials are new age materials exhibiting exceptional mechanical, electronic, and optical properties due to their unique structure and high surface-area to volume ratio [ [1] ]. Among nanomaterials, one dimensional (1D) metallic nanowires (NWs) are widely used for different applications including nanoelectronics, optoelectronics, energy harvesting and storage, ultrasensitive sensing, and nanoelectromechanical devices [ [2] , [3] , [4] ]. At the nanoscale, 1D NWs usually exhibit ultra high strength, differently from bulk materials, which makes them ideal candidates for studying their fundamental deformation mechanisms. Dislocation nucleation from free surfaces and its subsequent propagation through NWs has been found to be a dominant deformation mechanism in metallic NWs such as Au, Ag, Cu, and Ni [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. This enables reorientation to a more preferred phase, resulting in exceptional mechanical properties such as superplasticity, high yielding strength, pseudoelasticity, and shape memory effects [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ].

At 77 K, Ag NW deforms via nucleation and propagation of a partial dislocation from the free surface, leaving a stacking fault inside the NW (see Figure 3 a). As deformation continues, the stacking fault further separates into two twin boundaries, which extend and continue to grow through entire NW. The cross-section area of the NW eventually converts from (110) to (100), resulting in two peaks in the SS curve, as shown in Figure 2 a. The area between two twin boundaries is transformed as also shown in Figure 3 a between 8% to 32% elongation in the Ag NW. decision.trend: Early simulation studies on FCC high‐entropy alloys (such as the Cantor alloy) examined how intrinsic factors – like stacking fault energy and dislocation interactions influenced by longitudinal spin fluctuations – determine deformation behavior. Later work, including nanoscale investigations comparing HEA nanowires to classical FCC metals (e.g., Ag), clarified that the abundant slip systems in FCC lattices allow for multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocation glide, twinning, martensitic transformation) that underlie high ductility. In short, researchers moved from pure atomistic insights to integrated studies that reveal how the FCC structure promotes dislocation mobility and the absorption of deformation.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, the detailed mechanism linking the stacking fault energy and other dislocation‐mediated processes to the macroscopic ductility remains incomplete. In particular, under typical ambient conditions the precise way in which FCC microstructural features stabilize severe plastic deformation before fracture is not fully resolved.
decision.lever: Conduct in situ nano-mechanical testing (e.g., via TEM or synchrotron-based diffraction during tensile deformation) on a prototypical FCC alloy such as CoCrFeMnNi (the Cantor alloy) alongside advanced atomistic simulations to directly correlate stacking fault energy, dislocation behavior, and ductility metrics.
decision.why: This integrated approach naturally extends the current trend from simulation-only or isolated experimental studies. By targeting a well-known, highly ductile FCC system, it directly addresses the open mechanistic link between microstructural features (such as multiple slip systems and stacking fault energy) and superior ductility, in line with the cues of the research question and limitations of past studies.
